summary: Specifies how to aggregate end-to-end RSVP reservations over MPLS traffic engineering tunnels, including Diffserv-aware tunnels. It builds on RFC 3175, which handles aggregation over aggregate RSVP reservations.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of keeping track of each person's reserved seat, a bus company reserves a block of seats for a whole group. This does that for network bandwidth reservations over MPLS tunnels.

questions: rsvp aggregation over mpls te tunnels
how does rsvp work over mpls te tunnels
what is an rsvp aggregator and deaggregator
subtitle: How a handful of MPLS traffic engineering tunnels can stand in for thousands of individual RSVP reservations across a network core.

tldr.problem: Per-flow RSVP reservations give applications admission control, but routers in a large core cannot keep state for every flow.
tldr.mechanism: The router at the edge of the core (the Aggregator, which is also an MPLS TE tunnel Head-end) maps each end-to-end reservation onto a pre-established MPLS TE or DS-TE tunnel and does the admission control against that tunnel's reserved bandwidth. Core routers only see the tunnels.
tldr.outcome: A very large number of flows can be admitted in a scalable way, because the core is unaware of the end-to-end reservations. The RFC covers pre-established tunnels and unicast sessions only.

facts.label: IP protocol number on E2E Path

today: RFC 4804 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 3175, and the text leaves dynamically established tunnels and multicast aggregation for further study.

sections.title: Why Aggregate RSVP Over MPLS Tunnels
sections.content:
Integrated Services (Intserv) with RSVP lets applications ask the network for resources and be explicitly admitted or rejected. Differentiated Services (Diffserv) scales well because it sorts packets into a few classes by their Diffserv codepoint (DSCP) and needs no per-flow state, but it has no way for applications to talk to the network.

RFC 3175 already describes aggregating end-to-end RSVP reservations over aggregate RSVP reservations. RFC 4804 does the same thing over MPLS Traffic Engineering (TE) tunnels, including Diffserv-aware (DS-TE) tunnels. A TE tunnel is already an admission-controlled bandwidth reservation, it is signaled with RSVP, and packet scheduling in the core relies on Diffserv only. That makes it a natural fit for the aggregate reservation.

The document keeps the procedures of RFC 3175 and changes them only where tunnels require it. The main change is that jobs RFC 3175 gives to the Deaggregator, such as mapping reservations and resizing the aggregate, move to the Aggregator, because a TE tunnel is controlled by its Head-end.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping a note for every traveler in the middle of the network is too much work. So the edge router books a big block on a tunnel and the middle only knows about the block.

sections.title: Roles and Reference Model
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few roles. The Aggregator is at the ingress edge of the aggregation region and is also the TE tunnel Head-end. The Deaggregator is at the egress edge and is also the Tail-end. A Transit LSR is a Label Switch Router on the tunnel path that is neither. An E2E reservation is an RSVP reservation whose Path messages start upstream of the Aggregator and end downstream of the Deaggregator, and which is aggregated over a TE tunnel between them. E2E reservations are unidirectional, as in normal RSVP.

An E2E reservation may be a per-flow reservation, or itself an aggregate such as an aggregate IP reservation or an aggregate IPsec reservation. The text builds on the "RSVP over Tunnels" ideas of RFC 2746, but differs in several ways: it works over MPLS rather than IP tunnels (so penultimate hop popping must be handled), MPLS TE tunnels inherently reserve resources, there is exactly one aggregate reservation per tunnel, a tunnel is assumed to carry only reserved traffic, and several tunnels may share the same Head-end and Tail-end with Head-end policy choosing among them.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a doorman where the traffic enters the tunnel and another where it leaves. The first one decides which tunnel each group uses and checks there is still room.

sections.title: Path and Resv Handling with Pre-established Tunnels
sections.content:
The detailed procedures assume the TE tunnels already exist, whether set up by hand or through an automatic mesh. Dynamically established tunnels are left for further study. The procedures follow RFC 4206.

When an E2E Path message reaches the Aggregator, it MUST first map the reservation onto a TE tunnel, using routing information and local policy (for example Intserv service type, application identity or preemption priority). The choice can be tentative if more than one tunnel could apply. The Aggregator SHOULD update the ADSPEC to reflect the effect of the MPLS TE cloud, then MUST send the Path message addressed directly to the Deaggregator, with an IF_ID RSVP_HOP object that identifies the TE tunnel. Router Alert is not set, so transit LSRs do not see the message and the IP protocol number stays "RSVP" instead of being changed to "RSVP-E2E-IGNORE". The Deaggregator skips the IP TTL versus RSVP TTL check and forwards the Path message toward the receiver with Router Alert set.

The receiver's E2E Resv message goes back to the Deaggregator, which does ordinary admission control for its downstream segment and forwards it to the Aggregator. The Aggregator MUST make the final tunnel mapping, work out the request size from the Sender Tspec and Flowspec, and compare it with the tunnel's available bandwidth. If there is enough, it MUST record the use and forward the Resv upstream. If not, the reservation is not installed and a ResvError goes back toward the receiver. If the final mapping picks a different tunnel from the tentative one, the Aggregator MUST first resend the E2E Path with the new tunnel identified, and then either drop the Resv or continue processing it.

The Aggregator may resize a tunnel under various policies, from configuration only to dynamic increases, and SHOULD use make-before-break from RFC 3209 to change a tunnel's bandwidth. PathTear and ResvConf messages are forwarded like Path messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The first doorman picks a tunnel, then waits for the answer coming back. If the tunnel still has room, the request goes through. If not, the answer is no.

sections.title: Data Forwarding and Teardown
sections.content:
When the Aggregator receives a data packet that belongs to an E2E reservation currently mapped to a tunnel, it MUST encapsulate the packet into that TE tunnel. If the Aggregator and Deaggregator also act as IPsec Security Gateways, the packet is first encapsulated into the IPsec tunnel to the Deaggregator and then sent into the TE tunnel.

E2E reservations are removed the usual way: PathTear, ResvTear, timeout or error. The Aggregator MUST then update its local view of what is free on the tunnel. If a TE tunnel disappears because of a configuration, route or policy change, the Aggregator acts like an RSVP router facing a link failure. It may move the Path messages to another tunnel if routing and policy permit, or send Path_Error messages to the sender. State left on the old Deaggregator times out because it is no longer refreshed.
sections.plainLanguage: Once a seat is booked, the traveler's packets ride inside the tunnel. When someone cancels, the doorman crosses them off the count.

sections.title: IP Versions and Reservation Types
sections.content:
The procedures apply to IPv4 E2E reservations over IPv4 TE tunnels and to IPv6 over IPv6. IPv6 reservations over IPv4 tunnels also work, provided a mechanism such as 6PE (RFC 4798) routes the IPv6 traffic over the IPv4 MPLS core. The reverse case, IPv4 reservations over IPv6 tunnels, likewise needs a mechanism to route IPv4 over IPv6 MPLS.

The E2E reservation can be a per-flow reservation identified by the usual 5-tuple, an aggregate reservation identified by source address, destination address and DSCP as in RFC 3175, or a reservation for an IPsec-protected flow identified by source address, destination address and SPI as in RFC 2207. Like RFC 3175, this document covers unicast sessions only; multicast aggregation is for further study.
sections.plainLanguage: It works for both kinds of network addresses, and for single calls or whole groups of calls bundled together.

sections.title: Example Deployments
sections.content:
The first example is admission control of voice and video where there are very many hosts. Each host makes per-flow reservations for its video streams, audio streams and voice calls. The mapping policy might send audio and voice reservations to DS-TE tunnels of Class-Type 1 and video reservations to tunnels of Class-Type 0.

The second is voice call admission control in large telephony trunking networks. A trunk VoIP gateway can make one aggregate RSVP reservation for all calls toward another gateway, resized in steps as the call count changes. Tunnel Head-ends then act as Aggregators and admit those gateway reservations into MPLS TE tunnels, which may be protected by MPLS Fast Reroute.

Two appendices are informational. Appendix A shows how an RSVP proxy on the Aggregator can reserve over the tunnel on behalf of the far host, keeping RSVP signaling local between hosts and the edge router, which can shorten reservation set-up delay. Appendix B walks through VoIP call admission control where two gateways connect to edge routers PE1 and PE2 joined by DS-TE tunnels in each direction.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone companies and video-call systems can use this to make sure there is still room on the big pipe before they let another call start.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RSVP messages control reservations both outside the MPLS region (for E2E flows) and inside it (for TE tunnels). Their hop-by-hop integrity and node authentication can be protected with the mechanisms of RFC 2747 and RFC 3097. For E2E messages crossing the MPLS region, the Aggregator and Deaggregator act as RSVP neighbors and need a pre-shared secret.

Traffic in a TE tunnel can only be filtered by MPLS label, not by 5-tuple, so an administrator may wish to limit the domain where such tunnels can be set up. Because many E2E flows share one aggregate, compromising an aggregate has a multiplying effect; restricting this document to pre-established tunnels reduces that risk. If Aggregators resize tunnels dynamically, tunnels could hog core resources or cause heavy signaling and path churn, which configuration limits (maximum size, maximum resizing frequency) and TE preemption can mitigate. The protocol-number issue of RFC 3175 does not apply, since the number is not changed here.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone tricks the doorman, many travelers are affected at once. So the messages should be signed, and the tunnels should not be allowed to grow without limits.
